newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Protesters jam streets of Bulgaria's second city.
newsitem.headline: Protesters jam streets of Bulgaria's second city.

text.p: Tens of thousands of people joined an anti-government rally on Monday in Bulgaria's second city Plovdiv, the birthplace a week ago of the country's wave of unrest.

The peaceful march was among about 20 mass demonstrations reported in provincial towns and cities on Monday, as the ripples of an explosion of popular anger appeared to spread wider across the country.

Led by Orthodox priests, opposition deputies and the mayors of Plovdiv and Stara Zagora, the Plovdiv crowds angrily abused the beleaguered Socialist government for the beatings of protesters in Sofia as well as for Bulgaria's dire economic straits.
Students from Plovdiv's universities walked through the city centre carrying a portrait of Bulgarian president-elect Petar Stoyanov, an opposition politician born in the city.
Scores of riot and regular police stood guard as the march passed the Socialists' local headquarters.
Opposition stewards formed a human chain to separate demonstrators from police and prevent violence. But some students succeeded in handing carnations to security men.
Taxis blocked streets, residents hung out of windows to wave support, music shops blared pop music, and students leapt into the air chanting: "Those who don't jump are red". Everyone jumped.
"One cannot live in such poverty any more, there is no normal standard of living," said Tanya Raleva, an English language student at Plovdiv University.
"I have been abroad and I know their standard of living. We have either to leave the country or to demonstrate that a change is necessary."

Nikolai Todorov, 21, added: "Things have to change, because I fear that pretty soon we'll die of hunger. The ruling power should be changed because it proved it could not do anything positive for this country.
Real wages have plummeted and Bulgaria's lev currency has collapsed in recent months under the rule of the Socialists, the former Communists, who won parliamentary elections in 1994.
Deljan Arsenov, 16, from Plovdiv's gipsy quarter of Izgrev, said his mother was working for 7-8,000 levs a month, worth little more than $10, while a loaf of bread costs 120 levs.
"We cannot study because we have to work. We came here to shout," he said.
"Some of my neighbours even started stealing bread. Everything is so expensive that we don't have money even to buy a pair of trousers."
As well as chants of "mafia" and "red rubbish", marchers cried that the Socialists were "killers" after police beatings of opposition protesters in the capital Sofia on Saturday put some in hospital.

"On Saturday morning in Sofia we saw the blood of the Sofia children and we want all those who gave the orders to the police to be punished," said Muravei Radev, a parliamentary deputy of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF).
"Those who decided that with clubs they could shut the mouths of the hungry people, haven't they understood that their time is over?"
The mayor of Plovdiv, Spas Garnevski, was also clubbed when the Sofia demonstration was crushed on Saturday.

Marching among a sea of opposition blue banners, Bulgarian national flags, torches and candles, the deputy chairman of the UDF in Plovdiv, Velislav Velichkov, warned the next step would be a general strike unless the Socialists agreed to early elections. Later on Monday the government said it was prepared to discuss holding elections.
Old enough to remember the Communists' accession to power after World War Two, Georgi Karakolev, 72, marched with his wife.
"People die but they (the Communists) do not step down. Shame on them. They have exported Bulgaria, they have devoured it. Forty five years were not enough for them," he said.
